newsitem.title: USA: Election could help some funds, hurt others.
newsitem.headline: Election could help some funds, hurt others.

text.p: The presidential election could have a significant impact on your mutual fund portfolio in the coming years.
So while you're deciding whether to vote for President Clinton or Bob Dole, you should also be reviewing moves you might make in your investment portfolio after the election.

Traditionally, Wall Streeters have favoured Republicans, who are seen as stricter stewards of the economy, who will rein in taxes on wealthy investors and corporations and find ways to keep inflation at bay -- even if that means maintaining a tight rein on economic growth.
By contrast, professional investors often shun Democratic tickets due to concern that the Democrats will pursue policies unfavourable to business and investment.
But some money managers figure that a Clinton victory will be good news for at least one sector of the investment market -- small company stocks and the funds that invest in them.
A recent study by Liberty Financial Cos. analysed the gains by small company stocks during Republican and Democratic administrations since 1929.

It found that small stocks have climbed an average of 17.2 percent annually under Democratic administrations since the end of the Depression in 1937, but only 10.2 percent under Republicans during the same period.

The results from the start of the Hoover administration in 1929 are even more dramatic: Small stocks rose 22.8 percent annually for Democratic administrations versus only 1.9 percent for Republican administrations.
The trend has held up in recent times. Small stocks have gained 19.9 percent annually during Clinton's term, versus just 13.3 percent a year during the combined terms of Reagan and Bush.
Why the gap?

"It's generally accepted that Republican administrations are good for big business, but the Democratic focus on reducing unemployment tends to help small business," said Kenneth Leibler, Liberty's president and CEO.
"Investors might be well-served by including funds with a small-stock bias in their portfolios under a Democratic president."

Trouble is, many top-flight small company funds have shut their doors to new investors during recent years. The reason: As their coffers swell with new cash to invest, it becomes harder to find enough good small stocks to put that money to work.
For example, a manager who tries to invest significant sums in a stock with a market capitalisation of below $200 million or so will drive the price higher before he completes the purchases.

Some small company funds have kept their doors open to new investors, letting new money inflate their asset bases. In some cases, their performances have begun to slip; in others, the fund manager has been forced to buy shares of larger companies.
That said, there are still some potential winners among funds that buy small company shares.

Annette Larson, an analyst at Morningstar Mutual Funds in Chicago, likes PBHG Emerging Growth (800-433-0051; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load), which invests 65 percent of its assets in U.S. companies with market capitalisations ranging from $10 million to $250 million.
She also recommends Loomis Sayles Small Cap (800-633-3330; $2,500 minimum; no-load). It invests two-thirds of its assets in companies with market capitalisations of less than $500 million.

One new entry is also worth at least a look. Heartland Small Cap Contrarian (800-432-7856; $1,000 minimum; 0.25 percent load), managed by the same folks who brought us top-performer Heartland Value -- now closed, alas -- invests 65 percent of its assets in companies with market capitalisations of less than $500 million.
The fund also can invest 35 percent of its assets in high-yield bonds.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
